notes.meaning: David counted the men who had joined him and put officers over groups of a hundred and a thousand. Many fighters from the nearby tribes east of the Jordan came to help him, because they could not stand a son turning on his father. He split the army into three parts under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, and offered to march out and share the danger himself.

The people begged David to stay behind. The enemy cared most about killing the king, and he was worth ten thousand of them. He could help better from the city, keeping some troops ready to send if needed. It shows how dear a good ruler is to his people.

David gave in and stood by the gate as the troops marched past. Matthew Henry says it is wise to listen to good advice, even from those under us. He adds that God's care was at work too. If David had been in the battle, he would surely have tried to save Absalom.

David ordered his generals, in everyone's hearing, to be gentle with Absalom. That meant capture him but do not kill him. His reasons were a father's love, Absalom's youth, his sense that his own sins had brought on this revolt, and a wish that Absalom would have time to repent. Absalom wanted only David killed, while David wanted only Absalom spared. Matthew Henry sees in this a picture of God's mercy to rebels, like Jesus praying, "Father, forgive them."

David's army went out to fight "Israel," meaning the people who had followed Absalom. The battle was in the forest of Ephraim. Where exactly that forest was is debated. Many place it east of the Jordan, while Keil and Delitzsch place it in Ephraim's own land west of the river.

Absalom's side lost badly, with twenty thousand men killed. The large number shows how many people had joined the revolt. Matthew Henry says they paid a heavy price for turning against their rightful king. They were likely beaten by a smaller army, a sign that God was against them.

The fighting spread across the whole area, and the forest "devoured" more men than the sword. Thick trees, pits and swamps trapped the fleeing men, and David's soldiers caught them. Some old translations say wild animals killed them. It was God fighting for David, yet a sad win, because the dead were David's own people.

As Absalom fled on his mule, his head got stuck in the thick branches of a big oak. The mule ran off and left him hanging. Many older writers think his long hair, which he was so proud of, got caught, so his pride became his ruin. Others point out the text only says his head was jammed in the branches. Matthew Henry says he hung between heaven and earth, as if unfit for either.

A soldier saw Absalom hanging and told Joab. Joab scolded him for not killing Absalom on the spot. He said he would have rewarded him with silver and a soldier's belt. Such a belt was a badge of honor, a bit like being made an officer.

The soldier said he would not touch the king's son even for a hundred times that much silver. Everyone had heard David's order. The king would find out, and Joab himself would have turned against him. This man is a good picture of a loyal subject who respects the king's wishes more than money.

Joab refused to waste more time and thrust three spears or sharp sticks into Absalom while he was still alive. "Heart" here may mean the middle of his body, since he did not die at once. Commentators are torn about Joab. He openly disobeyed his king, and Adam Clarke calls it a cowardly murder. Yet others say he acted for the good of king and country, and Absalom had deserved death under God's law. David never forgot it (1 Kings 2:5).
Joab's spears did not finish Absalom off. So ten young men who carried Joab's weapons surrounded him and struck him until he died.
Joab blew the horn and called off the chase. With Absalom dead, the revolt was over and there was no need for more killing. He took pity on ordinary people who had been fooled by Absalom's flattery.

They threw Absalom's body into a pit in the forest and piled a huge heap of stones on it. That was a sign of shame, like the stone heap over Achan. It also showed he deserved to be stoned as a rebellious son (Deuteronomy 21:21). God turned his proud glory into disgrace. His followers ran home.

Earlier Absalom had set up a stone pillar for himself in the King's Valley near Jerusalem so he would be remembered. Earlier we read he had three sons (14:27), so they had probably died. The Geneva Notes see this as God's punishment. In the end a rough heap of stones became his real memorial, and his name is remembered with shame. The "Absalom's Tomb" shown today in that valley was built much later.

Ahimaaz, a young priest's son, wanted to run and tell David the good news that the LORD had rescued him. Joab said no, not today, because the king's son was dead. Joab cared about Ahimaaz and knew how hard David would take this news.
Joab sent a Cushite instead, a man from Cush (Ethiopia), probably a servant of Joab's. Joab had quietly told him that Absalom was dead.

Ahimaaz kept begging until Joab let him run too, though he had no real news to bring. He took the route across the plain and got there first. Matthew Henry suggests he may have wanted to show off his speed. Or he may have wanted to prepare David kindly before the hard news arrived.
David sat waiting in the space between the outer and inner gates of the city of Mahanaim. A watchman on the roof over the gate spotted a man running alone.

David reasoned that a man running alone must be a messenger with news. If the army had lost, crowds of men would be fleeing back. When a second runner appeared, he hoped this one also brought good news.
The watchman recognized Ahimaaz by the way he ran. David said he was a good man and must be bringing good news. He had proved loyal before, and Joab would hardly pick him to carry bad news.

Ahimaaz shouted "All is well!", bowed low, and praised the LORD for defeating the rebels. Like a true priest, he gave God the glory. By turning David first to thank God, he helped prepare him for the sad news to come.

David's first question was about Absalom. He was so much a father that he forgot he was a king. Ahimaaz gave a vague answer about a great uproar. Some think he really did not know. Many think he knew and dodged the question to avoid giving bad news, and some call that a lie.
David told Ahimaaz to step aside and wait. That way he could hear the second messenger and compare the two reports.

The Cushite arrived and announced that the LORD had rescued David from his enemies. When David asked about Absalom, he answered, "May all your enemies end up like that young man." It was polite and tactful, but it made plain that Absalom was dead.

David was shaken. He went up to the room over the gate to weep alone, crying, "My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you!" It is hard not to feel for him. Still, Matthew Henry, Wesley and Keil & Delitzsch think his grief went too far and kept him from seeing God's justice. The Geneva Notes add that he felt God's judgment on his own sin. Matthew Henry also sees in it a faint picture of the Savior, who wept over rebels and died for them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine said David stayed at peace with his son even in war, and only weep once peace came at the price of Absalom's death. He compared this to the Church grieving over those who are lost. Ambrose saw in the cry the deep grief over a sinner who died without repenting.
